title: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Board of Governors (1984)
shortTitle: Association of Data Processing Service Organizations v. Board of Governors (1984)
summary: The D.C. Circuit treated substantial evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review as requiring the same quantum of factual support, while distinguishing the record available for review.

sections.Parties: ADAPSO, a trade association for the data-processing industry, and two members challenged Federal Reserve Board orders benefiting Citicorp and bank holding companies. Citicorp intervened.
sections.Material Facts: Citicorp sought approval for its Citishare subsidiary to perform data-processing and transmission services and sell certain excess capacity and hardware. The Bank Holding Company Act allowed nonbanking activities closely related to banking. The Board also amended Regulation Y to permit such activities generally, subject to restrictions.
sections.Procedural History: An administrative law judge conducted a formal hearing addressing both the individual application and proposed regulatory changes. The Board approved the application and later adopted regulatory amendments. The D.C. Circuit consolidated petitions challenging the adjudicatory order and the notice-and-comment rule. The assigned excerpt addresses the standard of review; it omits the resolution of the underlying merits.
sections.Issue: Did factual findings underlying the individual approval and the general rule receive different evidentiary scrutiny, and what did the statute’s substantial-evidence requirement demand?
sections.Holding: The statute applied substantial-evidence review to both orders. The court held that this statutory standard demanded the same quantum of factual support as ordinary APA substantial-evidence review and, in its account, arbitrary-and-capricious review of factual support.
sections.Reasoning: Scalia explained that § 706’s provisions are cumulative: evidence may be sufficient yet agency action still arbitrary for an unexplained departure from precedent. When § 706(2)(E) does not apply, § 706(2)(A) still prevents decisions without adequate factual support. Formal proceedings constrain the supporting evidence to their closed record; an informal-action record can include what the agency actually considered, subject to applicable disclosure obligations. The editorial note identifies the general equivalence discussion as technically dictum in this case because the organic statute already supplied one standard. It also notes that the Supreme Court has not squarely resolved the precise equivalence issue and that differently worded or understood organic statutes may demand more stringent review. This case is distinct from the 1970 Data Processing standing case.
